nodes.name: Krishna
nodes.description: The eighth son of Vasudeva and Devaki, raised among the cowherds of Vraja, who became the prince of the Yadavas at Dvaraka, the friend and charioteer of Arjuna and the teacher of the Bhagavad Gita. Revered as the eighth (or ninth) avatar of Vishnu, and in several Vaishnava schools as the Supreme Lord himself, he is among the most widely worshipped figures of Hinduism.
nodes.story: When a heavenly voice warned Kamsa that Devaki's eighth child would kill him, he imprisoned Devaki and Vasudeva in Mathura and killed their newborns one by one; the seventh embryo, Balarama, was secretly drawn into Rohini's womb. At midnight on the eighth day of the dark fortnight Krishna was born, first revealing a four-armed divine form before becoming an ordinary infant. The guards sank into sleep and the prison doors opened. Vasudeva carried the child through a storm across the Yamuna, which gave way before him, and exchanged him for the newborn daughter of Yashoda in Gokula. When Kamsa seized the girl to dash her against a stone, she slipped from his grasp, rose into the sky as the Goddess, and told him that his destroyer was already alive and safe.
nodes.abode: Mathura, Vraja (Gokula and Vrindavan) and Dvaraka; Goloka in devotional theology
sources: Mahabharata (esp. Sabha, Udyoga, Bhishma and Mausala Parvas)
variations: Chandogya Upanishad 3.17.6 mentions a 'Krishna Devakiputra', pupil of Ghora Angirasa; whether he is the same figure as the epic Krishna is debated.
Panini's grammar (4.3.98) refers to devotion to Vasudeva, and the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar (c. 2nd century BCE) calls Vasudeva 'god of gods', attesting an early Bhagavata cult.
Many scholars see a fusion of Vasudeva-Krishna of the Vrishni clan, the epic hero of the Mahabharata and the pastoral Gopala-Krishna of the Harivamsha and Puranas.
The Mahabharata (Adi Parva) and Vishnu Purana say Vishnu plucked a black hair and a white hair, which became Krishna and Balarama.
Gaudiya and other Krishna-centred schools, citing Bhagavata 1.3.28 ('krishnas tu bhagavan svayam'), hold that Krishna is not an avatar but the source of all avatars, including Vishnu.
The Bhagavata counts 16,108 wives (eight principal queens plus 16,100 women freed from Narakasura); other texts give different figures.
Jain tradition makes Krishna the ninth and last Vasudeva of this age and a cousin of the Tirthankara Neminatha; a Buddhist Jataka (Ghata Jataka) retells his family saga.

nodes.name: Balarama
nodes.description: Krishna's elder brother, a son of Vasudeva conceived in Devaki's womb and transferred to that of Rohini, famed for immense strength, his plough and pestle and his love of wine. He is regarded as an incarnation of the cosmic serpent Shesha and, in many lists, as an avatar of Vishnu; he taught Bhima and Duryodhana the mace and refused to fight at Kurukshetra.
nodes.story: Once, returning to Vraja and warm with the wine Varuni, Balarama wandered by the Yamuna with the cowherd women and called on the river to come near so that he could bathe. The Yamuna ignored the words of one who seemed drunk. Enraged, Balarama hooked her with the tip of his plough and dragged her towards him, threatening to split her into a hundred streams. Terrified, the river goddess appeared before him, fell at his feet and begged forgiveness, praising him as Ananta, the serpent who bears the earth. Balarama released her, and she bathed and adorned him; the Puranas say the Yamuna still bends along the course his plough carved. The episode shows the elder brother's dual nature: a rustic, hot-tempered hero who is at the same time the cosmic Shesha.
variations: The Harivamsha says the goddess Nidra (Vishnu's Sleep) transferred the embryo from Devaki to Rohini; the Bhagavata names Yogamaya.

Mahabharata and Vishnu Purana: Balarama arose from a white hair of Vishnu; elsewhere he is the incarnation of Shesha. In the Mausala Parva, at his death a great white serpent leaves his mouth and enters the ocean.
Dashavatara lists vary: some include Balarama as the eighth avatar with Krishna as the source of all, others replace Balarama with Buddha; the Gita Govinda includes both Balarama and Buddha.
In Pancharatra theology he is Sankarshana, the second of the four vyuhas; scholars link him to an early agricultural deity.
Jain tradition makes him the ninth Baladeva. The daughter Vatsala/Shashirekha of the Maya Bazaar story belongs to regional folk tradition, not the Sanskrit texts.

nodes.name: Revati
nodes.description: Wife of Balarama, daughter of King Kakudmi (Raivata) of Kushasthali, the city later rebuilt as Dvaraka. Her story, in which ages pass on earth during a short visit to Brahma's world, is one of the earliest descriptions of time dilation in world literature.
nodes.story: King Kakudmi, a descendant of Vaivasvata Manu, could find no man worthy of his beautiful daughter Revati, so he took her to Brahmaloka to ask the Creator himself. Brahma was listening to the Gandharvas sing, and the king waited politely until the performance ended before making his request. Brahma laughed: in the brief moment they had waited, twenty-seven cycles of the four yugas had passed on earth; every suitor Kakudmi had in mind, and their descendants and kingdoms, had long vanished. He advised the king to return and give Revati to Balarama, a portion of Vishnu now living on earth. Revati, from an earlier age, was far taller than the people of the new era, so Balarama gently pressed her down with the tip of his plough until she was of ordinary height, and they were married.
variations: The shrinking of Revati with the plough appears in the Vishnu Purana and later retellings but not in the Bhagavata's account.
Her sons with Balarama are named Nishatha and Ulmuka.

nodes.name: Devaki
nodes.description: Mother of Krishna, daughter of Devaka (brother of King Ugrasena) and wife of Vasudeva. Imprisoned by her cousin Kamsa, she lost six sons to him before Krishna was born and smuggled away; she is revered as the rebirth of Aditi, mother of the gods.
nodes.story: Years after Krishna had grown to be lord of Dvaraka, Devaki still mourned the six sons Kamsa had slain in the prison at Mathura. Having seen her sons bring back their guru's dead child from Yama's realm, she begged Krishna and Balarama to let her see her lost children again. The brothers entered Sutala, the underworld kingdom of Bali, who welcomed them with reverence, and brought back the six boys. They had once been sons of the sage Marichi, cursed to be born among asuras and then of Devaki. When Devaki embraced them, milk flowed from her breasts; she nursed them, and touched by the remnants of Krishna's own nourishment the boys were freed from their curse. They bowed to their parents and to Krishna and rose to the heavens, leaving Devaki consoled.
variations: Harivamsha: Aditi and Surabhi were reborn as Devaki and Rohini after Brahma cursed Kashyapa (reborn as Vasudeva) for taking Varuna's cows.
Bhagavata 10.3: in earlier ages Devaki and Vasudeva were Prishni and Sutapa, then Aditi and Kashyapa, and each time Vishnu was born as their son.
The return of her six slain sons is told only in the Bhagavata (10.85).

nodes.name: Vasudeva
nodes.description: The Yadava (Vrishni) prince who fathered Krishna and Balarama, son of Shurasena and brother of Kunti. His epithet Anakadundubhi recalls the celestial drums that sounded at his birth; his patronymic gave Krishna the name Vasudeva (with a long a).
nodes.story: At Vasudeva's wedding to Devaki, her cousin Kamsa was driving the bridal chariot when a voice from the sky declared that her eighth child would kill him. Kamsa seized his cousin by the hair and drew his sword. Vasudeva calmly reasoned with him: killing a bride on her wedding day would bring infamy, and death comes to all in any case; the danger lay not in Devaki but in her children, and he swore to hand over every one of them. Kamsa relented. When their first son was born, Vasudeva, true to his word, carried the infant to Kamsa, who was moved and returned the child. But when Narada later reminded Kamsa that the Yadavas were gods born to destroy him, Kamsa threw the couple in chains and began killing their sons, setting the stage for Krishna's secret birth.
variations: Harivamsha: Vasudeva is the rebirth of Kashyapa, cursed by Brahma to be born as a cowherd-king for stealing Varuna's cows; Bhagavata: of Prajapati Sutapa and then Kashyapa.
Lists of his wives differ: the Bhagavata names Rohini, Devaki and several of Devaki's sisters among others.
Mahabharata, Mausala Parva: he died of grief after the destruction of the Yadavas, and four of his wives entered his funeral pyre.

nodes.name: Shurasena
nodes.description: A Yadava king of the Vrishni branch, father of Vasudeva and of Pritha (Kunti), and thus grandfather of both Krishna and the Pandavas. His name also belongs to the Shurasena country around Mathura.
nodes.story: Shura, chief of the Vrishnis, was bound by friendship to his cousin Kuntibhoja, who had no children. Keeping a promise made long before, Shura gave his firstborn daughter Pritha to Kuntibhoja to raise as his own, and so she became known as Kunti. In her adoptive father's house she served the irascible sage Durvasa so well that he taught her the mantra by which she later called down the gods and bore Karna and the Pandavas. Shura's son Vasudeva was born to great portents: the gods, knowing that Vishnu would take birth in his house, sounded their kettledrums in the heavens, and the child was named Anakadundubhi. Through this one king the two great lines of the epics, the Pandavas and the family of Krishna, are joined as cousins.
variations: The Mahabharata usually calls him Shura; Shurasena is also the name of the Mathura region and of an earlier king of the Yadu line.
The Bhagavata makes him son of Devamidha; genealogies of the Yadavas differ considerably between the Puranas.

nodes.name: Nanda
nodes.description: Chief of the cowherds of Gokula and Vraja, husband of Yashoda and foster father of Krishna. A friend of Vasudeva, he raised Krishna as his own son; in devotional traditions he embodies parental love (vatsalya) for God.
nodes.story: After fasting on the Ekadashi, Nanda entered the Yamuna before dawn to bathe, not noticing that the auspicious hour had not yet begun. A servant of Varuna, lord of the waters, seized him and dragged him down to Varuna's palace. The cowherds on the shore cried out for Krishna, who plunged into the river and came before Varuna. The god of the ocean received him with the highest worship, begged forgiveness for his servant's ignorance, and returned Nanda at once. Back on the bank, Nanda told the astonished villagers of the splendour of Varuna's court and how its lord had bowed before his little son. The cowherds began to wonder whether Krishna was really God, and Krishna, to fulfil their longing, showed them a vision of his own spiritual realm.
variations: Bhagavata 10.8: Nanda and Yashoda were the Vasu Drona and his wife Dhara, who received from Brahma the boon of pure devotion to Hari on earth.
The rescue from Varuna (Bhagavata 10.28) and the swallowing of Nanda by a python (10.34) are Bhagavata episodes.

Some Gaudiya Vaishnava commentators hold that Krishna was also born to Yashoda alongside Yogamaya, making the Krishna of Vraja truly Nanda's son (Vrajendra-nandana); mainstream texts treat Nanda as foster father.

nodes.name: Yashoda
nodes.description: Wife of Nanda and foster mother of Krishna in Gokula, to whom the infant was secretly brought on the night of his birth. Her tender, scolding love for the child-god is celebrated in the Bhagavata, Surdas and countless devotional songs.
nodes.story: One day the cowherd boys ran to Yashoda crying that little Krishna had eaten mud. She caught him by the hand and scolded him, but he denied it: they were lying, he said, and she could look for herself. Yashoda told him to open his mouth. Inside, she saw the whole universe: the heavens and the directions, mountains, islands and oceans, the moving and unmoving beings, the elements, time and nature, and even Vraja and herself standing before her child. Bewildered, she wondered whether it was a dream, a delusion or her son's divine power, and she bowed to the Lord who is beyond thought. Then Krishna spread his Yogamaya over her again; she forgot what she had seen, lifted him onto her lap and loved him as her own little boy once more.
variations: The girl born to Yashoda and exchanged for Krishna is Nidra/Ekanamsha in the Harivamsha and Yogamaya in the Bhagavata; she is later worshipped as Vindhyavasini.
Bhagavata 10.8: Yashoda was formerly Dhara, wife of the Vasu Drona.

nodes.name: Radha
nodes.description: The cowherd maiden of Vraja who is Krishna's supreme beloved, worshipped as the embodiment of devotional love (prema) and, in several Vaishnava schools, as Krishna's own divine energy of bliss (hladini shakti), inseparable from him. Radha and Krishna together are adored as the divine couple (Radha-Krishna, Yugala).
nodes.story: Jayadeva's Gita Govinda sings of a spring night in Vrindavan when Radha finds Krishna dancing and playing with the other cowherd women. Wounded, she withdraws into a bower and pines for him, while Krishna, remembering her alone among all, wanders the banks of the Yamuna repentant and lovesick. Radha's confidante goes back and forth between them bearing messages. At dawn Krishna comes to her, but Radha, still hurt, turns him away. At last, when her anger has melted into longing, the friend leads her to the bower where he waits, and the two are reunited in joy. Tradition says Jayadeva hesitated to write the verse in which Krishna asks to place Radha's foot upon his head; returning from his bath he found it written in his manuscript by Krishna himself.
symbols: blue garment (in contrast to Krishna's yellow)
nodes.abode: Barsana and Vrindavan in Vraja; Goloka in devotional theology
sources: Brahmavaivarta Purana (Krishna Janma and Prakriti Khandas)
Works of the Gaudiya Gosvamins (e.g. Rupa Gosvami's Ujjvala Nilamani)
variations: Radha is absent by name from the Mahabharata, Harivamsha, Vishnu Purana and Bhagavata Purana; devotees read Bhagavata 10.30 (the gopi Krishna takes aside during the rasa dance, 'anayaradhito') as a veiled reference to her.

Early secular references appear in Prakrit poetry such as the Gatha Saptashati (early first millennium CE); she becomes central in Jayadeva's Gita Govinda (12th century) and the Brahmavaivarta Purana.

Brahmavaivarta: Radha emerges from Krishna's left side in Goloka, is cursed by Shridama to take birth on earth, and is married to Krishna by Brahma in the Bhandira forest; it also counts her among the five principal forms of Prakriti.
Nimbarka and Vallabha schools worship Radha with Krishna; Gaudiya Vaishnavism holds her to be Krishna's hladini shakti and the source of Lakshmi, and sees Chaitanya as Radha and Krishna combined.
Traditions differ on whether her love is svakiya (as wife) or parakiya (beyond marriage); some texts give her a husband (Ayana or Abhimanyu), while others deny this.
She is often described as a form of Lakshmi; in Shakta-influenced texts as a form of the Great Goddess.

nodes.name: Rukmini
nodes.description: Princess of Vidarbha, daughter of King Bhishmaka and sister of Rukmi, who became Krishna's first and chief queen at Dvaraka and mother of Pradyumna. She is revered as an incarnation of Lakshmi and worshipped with Vithoba at Pandharpur.
nodes.story: Rukmini had given her heart to Krishna from hearing of his virtues, but her brother Rukmi insisted she marry his friend Shishupala of Chedi, and the wedding was fixed. In despair she sent a trusted brahmin to Dvaraka with a letter: she had chosen Krishna as her husband; he should come and carry her off, not from the palace, where blood would be shed, but when she went out, as was custom, to worship the Goddess at her temple on the eve of the wedding. Krishna raced to Kundina. As Rukmini stepped out of the shrine, he lifted her into his chariot before the assembled kings. Rukmi pursued and was defeated; Krishna spared his life at Rukmini's plea, shaving his head in humiliation, and the couple were married in Dvaraka.
variations: The famous seven-verse letter to Krishna is found in the Bhagavata (10.52); the Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana tell the abduction without it.
Mahabharata, Mausala Parva: after Krishna's death Rukmini, with Jambavati and others, entered the funeral fire.
A Dvaraka tradition says Durvasa cursed Rukmini to live apart from Krishna, explaining her separate temple there.
The Tulabharam story, where Rukmini's single tulasi leaf outweighs Satyabhama's gold, is a regional devotional tale.

nodes.name: Satyabhama
nodes.description: Daughter of the Yadava noble Satrajit, owner of the Syamantaka jewel, and one of Krishna's principal queens. Proud and spirited, she rode with Krishna into battle against Narakasura and demanded the heavenly Parijata tree; many traditions see her as an incarnation of Bhudevi, the Earth.
nodes.story: After Krishna slew Narakasura and returned the stolen earrings of Aditi to heaven, Satyabhama, who had ridden with him on Garuda, saw the Parijata tree growing in Indra's garden, born from the churning of the ocean and fragrant beyond any earthly flower. She longed to plant it in her own courtyard at Dvaraka. Indra's queen Shachi, disdaining a mortal woman, would not share it. Krishna uprooted the tree and placed it on Garuda's back; when Indra and the gods pursued, he defeated them. Satyabhama then told Indra that she had wanted only to humble Shachi's pride and offered to give the tree back, but Indra, acknowledging Krishna, let it go. The Parijata was planted in Satyabhama's garden, to remain on earth only as long as Krishna did.
weapons: bow (in the Narakasura battle, in later retellings)
variations: Harivamsha: Narada brings a single Parijata blossom which Krishna gives to Rukmini; Satyabhama's jealousy prompts Krishna to fetch the whole tree. Vishnu Purana and Bhagavata set the episode after the killing of Narakasura, with Shachi refusing the flower.

Bhagavata 10.59: Krishna kills Narakasura while Satyabhama rides beside him on Garuda; regional traditions (especially in the south and in Deepavali lore) say Satyabhama herself killed Naraka, since as Bhudevi she was his mother and he could die only by her hand.
The Syamantaka jewel story (Harivamsha, Vishnu Purana 4.13, Bhagavata 10.56–57) explains how Satrajit gave her to Krishna.
Mahabharata, Mausala Parva: after Krishna's death she retired to the forest as an ascetic.
The Telugu Parijatapaharanamu of Nandi Timmana and the folk Tulabharam story are later regional works.

nodes.name: Jambavati
nodes.description: Daughter of the bear-king Jambavan and one of Krishna's principal queens, mother of Samba. She came to Krishna together with the Syamantaka jewel at the end of his long duel with her father.
nodes.story: When Prasena of the Yadavas went hunting wearing the radiant Syamantaka jewel, he was killed by a lion, and the lion in turn by Jambavan, the ancient king of the bears, who carried the gem to his cave. Dvaraka whispered that Krishna had killed Prasena for the jewel. To clear his name Krishna followed the tracks into the dark cave, where he found the jewel hanging as a plaything above a child's cradle while the nurse sang of it. Jambavan rushed at the intruder, and the two fought for twenty-eight days. At last the exhausted bear-king realised that only his lord Rama could match such strength; recognising Rama in Krishna, he bowed, returned the Syamantaka, and gave him his daughter Jambavati in marriage.
variations: The duel lasts twenty-one days in the Vishnu Purana and twenty-eight in the Bhagavata.
Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva: Krishna underwent austerities to Shiva, initiated by the sage Upamanyu, so that Jambavati might bear a son, and was blessed with Samba.
Mahabharata, Mausala Parva: she entered the funeral fire after Krishna's death.

nodes.name: Rukmi
nodes.description: Eldest son of King Bhishmaka of Vidarbha and brother of Rukmini, a mighty archer who owned the celestial bow Vijaya. A friend of Shishupala and Jarasandha and an implacable enemy of Krishna, he was killed by Balarama after a quarrel over dice.
nodes.story: When Krishna carried off Rukmini, her brother Rukmi swore before the kings that he would not return to Kundina until he had killed Krishna and brought his sister back. He overtook the chariot and fought furiously, but Krishna shattered his weapons and was about to kill him when Rukmini fell at Krishna's feet and begged for her brother's life. Krishna bound him and shaved his head and beard in patches, a humiliation Balarama rebuked as unworthy of kinsmen. Unable to go home, Rukmi founded the city of Bhojakata. Years later, at the wedding of his granddaughter Rochana to Krishna's grandson Aniruddha, he challenged Balarama to dice, cheated, and mocked him as a cowherd who knew nothing of the game. When a heavenly voice declared Balarama the winner, Rukmi jeered again, and Balarama struck him dead with his club.
variations: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva: a pupil of the Kimpurusha Druma, he owned Vijaya, one of three celestial bows with Gandiva and Sharnga; he offered his army first to Arjuna and then to Duryodhana, and both refused him because of his boasting, so he sat out the war.
His daughter Rukmavati married Pradyumna and his granddaughter Rochana married Aniruddha (Bhagavata 10.61).
Accounts of the dice game differ in detail; in several versions Balarama also knocks out the teeth of the king of Kalinga, who had laughed at him.

nodes.name: Pradyumna
nodes.description: The eldest son of Krishna and Rukmini, the rebirth of Kamadeva, the god of love, after Shiva burned him to ashes. Stolen as an infant by the demon Shambara, he grew up in the demon's house, killed him and returned to Dvaraka with Rati; in Pancharatra theology he is the third vyuha of Vishnu.
nodes.story: Kamadeva, burned by Shiva's third eye, was reborn as the son of Krishna and Rukmini. The demon Shambara, who knew the child would one day kill him, stole the baby from the birthing chamber within days of his birth and flung him into the sea. A great fish swallowed the child; fishermen caught it and presented it to Shambara, and when the cooks cut it open the boy was found alive inside. Shambara's housekeeper Mayavati, who was Rati awaiting her husband and had been told the truth by Narada, raised him. When he came of age she revealed who he was and taught him the magic that overcomes illusion. Pradyumna challenged Shambara, defeated all his sorceries and cut off his head, then flew with Rati to Dvaraka, where the women at first mistook him for Krishna himself.
variations: Accounts differ on how many days old he was when stolen (six in the Bhagavata, seven in some other texts).

In Pancharatra and Bhagavata theology the four vyuhas are Vasudeva, Sankarshana, Pradyumna and Aniruddha; a 1st-century CE inscription at Mora near Mathura honours five Vrishni heroes including Pradyumna and Samba.
He also married Rukmi's daughter Rukmavati. He was killed in the drunken brawl at Prabhasa (Mausala Parva).

nodes.name: Aniruddha
nodes.description: Son of Pradyumna and grandson of Krishna, the beloved of the asura princess Usha, whose secret marriage led to a great war between Krishna and Banasura, who was protected by Shiva. In Pancharatra theology he is the fourth vyuha of Vishnu.
nodes.story: Carried by magic from his bed in Dvaraka to the inner chambers of Usha in Shonitapura, Aniruddha lived there secretly with the princess who had dreamed of him. When her father Banasura's guards discovered the prince, Aniruddha seized an iron club and cut down all who attacked him, until the thousand-armed Bana bound him with serpent-weapons. At Dvaraka the Yadavas searched in vain for four months, until Narada told them where he was held. Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna marched on Shonitapura riding Garuda. Shiva himself came out to defend his devotee Bana with his ganas and fever-spirit, and the battle shook the worlds, until Krishna stunned Shiva with a weapon of yawning and began lopping off Bana's arms. At Shiva's plea Bana was spared, and Aniruddha and Usha returned to Dvaraka in honour.
variations: His first wife was Rochana, Rukmi's granddaughter (Bhagavata 10.61); his son Vajra survived the Mausala and was installed by Arjuna at Indraprastha.
Bhagavata 10.63 has Krishna leave Bana four arms; other texts give two.
In the Harivamsha the battle ends with Shiva and Krishna declaring their identity, a key Harihara passage.

nodes.name: Usha (daughter of Bana)
nodes.description: The daughter of the thousand-armed asura king Banasura of Shonitapura, who fell in love with Aniruddha after seeing him in a dream. Her secret union with Krishna's grandson provoked the war between Krishna and Bana; she is not to be confused with the Vedic dawn goddess Ushas.
nodes.story: Watching Shiva and Parvati together, the young Usha longed for a husband, and Parvati promised that she would meet him in a dream. One night a handsome youth came to her in sleep and vanished at dawn, leaving her desolate. Her friend Chitralekha, a gifted painter and yogini, drew portraits of every notable prince of gods, gandharvas and men; when she reached the Vrishnis, Usha blushed at the picture of Aniruddha, Krishna's grandson. That same night Chitralekha flew by her magic powers to Dvaraka and carried the sleeping prince on his bed back to Usha's palace. The two lived together in secret, hidden in the maiden's apartments, until her guards noticed the signs and informed Banasura, setting in motion a war that brought Krishna and Shiva face to face.
variations: The Harivamsha gives Parvati's promise and names the day of the dream; the Bhagavata tells the story more briefly.
Regional traditions place Shonitapura in Assam (Tezpur) or the Himalaya; in Gujarat she is Okha, and the Okhaharan is a popular folk narrative.

nodes.name: Samba
nodes.description: Son of Krishna and Jambavati, a handsome and headstrong Yadava prince whose prank on visiting sages brought down the curse of the iron pestle that destroyed the Yadava clan. Later tradition credits him with founding sun-worship at a temple on the Chandrabhaga after being healed of leprosy.
nodes.story: Some time after the great war, the sages Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada came to Dvaraka. The young Yadavas, bent on mockery, dressed Samba as a pregnant woman and presented him to the seers: this is the wife of Babhru, who longs for a son; tell us what she will bear. The sages saw through the insult and replied that she would bring forth a terrible iron pestle that would destroy the Vrishnis and Andhakas, sparing only Balarama and Krishna. The next day Samba delivered an iron club. King Ugrasena had it ground to powder and cast into the sea, and banned wine in the city, but rushes grew from the powder on the shore. Years later at Prabhasa, drunk and quarrelling, the Yadavas snatched up those rushes, which turned into iron clubs in their hands, and slaughtered one another.
variations: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva names Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada; Bhagavata 11.1 lists a larger group of sages at Pindaraka, including Durvasa, Bhrigu, Angiras, Kashyapa, Atri, Vashistha and Narada.

Bhagavata 10.68: Samba carried off Duryodhana's daughter Lakshmana from her svayamvara and was captured by the Kauravas; Balarama freed him by threatening to drag Hastinapura into the Ganga with his plough.

Samba and Bhavishya Puranas: Krishna cursed Samba with leprosy (after Narada engineered his presence among Krishna's wives); he was cured by worshipping Surya and founded a sun temple at Mitravana on the Chandrabhaga (associated with Multan and later with Konark).
The Mora well inscription near Mathura (1st century CE) honours him among the five Vrishni heroes.

nodes.name: Kamsa
nodes.description: The tyrant king of Mathura, son of Ugrasena, who imprisoned his own father, persecuted his cousin Devaki and tried repeatedly to kill the infant Krishna. Son-in-law and ally of Jarasandha, he was slain by Krishna in the wrestling arena of Mathura; the Puranas identify him as the reborn asura Kalanemi.
nodes.story: Failing to kill Krishna with demons in Vraja, Kamsa invited the brothers to a bow festival in Mathura, planning to finish them in the arena. At the gate the rogue elephant Kuvalayapida charged them; Krishna pulled out its tusk and killed it. Inside, the champion wrestlers Chanura and Mushtika fell to Krishna and Balarama. Furious, Kamsa ordered the cowherds driven out, Nanda arrested and Vasudeva and Ugrasena killed. Krishna leapt onto the royal dais, seized Kamsa by the hair as he raised his sword, flung him down into the arena and fell on him, crushing out his life. The Bhagavata adds that Kamsa, who had thought of Krishna night and day in fear, while eating, walking and sleeping, attained the same form as the Lord. Krishna freed his parents and restored Ugrasena to the throne.
variations: Harivamsha and Bhagavata 10.1: Kamsa was the rebirth of the asura Kalanemi, slain by Vishnu in an earlier age.
Some retellings make his real father the Danava Drumila, who seduced Ugrasena's queen in the king's form, explaining Kamsa's demonic nature.
His wives Asti and Prapti were daughters of Jarasandha, whose repeated attacks on Mathura avenged Kamsa's death.
Devaki is his cousin (daughter of Ugrasena's brother Devaka) but is often called his sister.

nodes.name: Jarasandha
nodes.description: The powerful emperor of Magadha, a devotee of Shiva and father-in-law of Kamsa, who besieged Mathura again and again and forced the Yadavas to move to Dvaraka. He was killed by Bhima in single combat with Krishna's guidance, opening the way for Yudhishthira's Rajasuya.
nodes.story: King Brihadratha of Magadha had no heir until the sage Chandakaushika gave him a blessed mango. The king divided it between his two queens, and each bore half a child: one eye, one arm, one leg. Horrified, the queens had the halves thrown out. A rakshasi named Jara found them and, to carry them more easily, pressed them together; the halves joined into a mighty, crying boy, who was named Jarasandha, 'joined by Jara'. Grown to be emperor, he imprisoned eighty-six kings to sacrifice to Rudra. Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna came to Girivraja disguised as brahmins and challenged him to single combat. Jarasandha chose Bhima. They wrestled for thirteen days and nights; on the fourteenth, as the king tired, Bhima lifted him, whirled him a hundred times and broke him, and the captive kings were freed.
variations: Bhagavata 10.72 and later retellings: Krishna signals to Bhima by splitting a twig, and Bhima tears Jarasandha into his two original halves; the Mahabharata has Bhima break him on his knee.

Bhagavata 10.50: Jarasandha attacked Mathura seventeen times and was defeated each time; on the eighteenth, allied with Kalayavana, Krishna moved the Yadavas to Dvaraka. Other texts give eighteen assaults.
Mahabharata, Shanti Parva: Karna once defeated Jarasandha in a wrestling bout and received the city of Malini from him.

nodes.name: Shishupala
nodes.description: King of Chedi, son of Damaghosha and of Shrutashrava, Vasudeva's sister, and thus Krishna's cousin. A general of Jarasandha and the rejected suitor of Rukmini, he insulted Krishna at Yudhishthira's Rajasuya and was beheaded by the Sudarshana discus.
nodes.story: Shishupala was born with three eyes and four arms, braying like an ass, and his parents wished to abandon him until a voice declared that the child was mighty, and that the one on whose lap his extra eye and arms fell away would be his slayer. When Krishna came to Chedi and took the baby on his lap, the extra limbs vanished. His aunt begged Krishna to spare her son, and he promised to forgive a hundred of Shishupala's offences. Years later, at the Rajasuya of Yudhishthira, Bhishma proposed that the first honour be given to Krishna. Shishupala rose in fury, reviling Krishna, Bhishma and the Pandavas and recounting slanders without end. When the hundredth offence was passed, Krishna released his discus and severed Shishupala's head; a radiance rose from the body and, before all the kings, entered Krishna.
variations: Bhagavata 7.1: Vishnu's gatekeepers Jaya and Vijaya, cursed by the Kumaras, were born as Hiranyakashipu and Hiranyaksha, then Ravana and Kumbhakarna, then Shishupala and Dantavakra; popular tradition identifies Shishupala with Jaya, though assignments vary.
Vishnu Purana 4.14–15 says the same being was Hiranyakashipu, then Ravana, then Shishupala, and was finally liberated by dying at Krishna's hand while thinking of him in hatred.
The Bhagavata gives him a birth tale in brief; the full account of the extra limbs is in the Mahabharata, Sabha Parva. Magha's 7th-century epic Shishupalavadha retells his death.

nodes.name: Putana
nodes.description: A demoness sent by Kamsa to kill the newborn children of Vraja, who tried to suckle the infant Krishna with poisoned breasts and had her life drawn out by him. Because she had offered him her breast, even as an enemy, the Bhagavata says she attained the realm of a mother.
nodes.story: Sent by Kamsa to kill every infant in the villages, Putana flew into Gokula and took the form of a lovely woman, her hair wreathed in jasmine. So charming was she that Yashoda and Rohini, dazzled, let her lift the baby Krishna from his cradle. She put him to her breast, smeared with deadly poison. Krishna, pressing her breast tight with both hands, sucked out her very life with the milk. Screaming 'let go, let go', she ran out, her true form bursting forth, and fell dead, her enormous body crushing trees for miles around. The terrified cowherds cut the corpse to pieces and burned it, and the smoke rose fragrant as aloe wood, because her body had been purified by nursing the Lord. The gopis then performed protective rites over the child.
variations: The Harivamsha calls her Kamsa's foster-nurse and describes her coming in the form of a bird (shakuni).
Bhagavata 10.6 describes her beauty, her giant corpse and her liberation to the destination of a mother.
Later devotional texts (e.g. the Garga Samhita) say she was formerly Ratnamala, daughter of Bali, who wished to nurse Vamana as her son.
In Ayurvedic texts such as the Sushruta Samhita, Putana is one of the grahas, spirits that afflict children.

nodes.name: Kaliya
nodes.description: A many-headed venomous naga who poisoned a pool of the Yamuna near Vrindavan, until the boy Krishna subdued him by dancing on his hoods. Spared at the plea of his wives, he was sent back to the island of Ramanaka, safe from Garuda.
nodes.story: Fleeing his enemy Garuda, Kaliya settled in a deep pool of the Yamuna where Garuda could not come, because the sage Saubhari had cursed him. The serpent's venom made the water boil; birds flying over fell dead and cows and cowherd boys who drank there collapsed. Krishna climbed a kadamba tree and leapt into the pool. Kaliya coiled around him while the people of Vraja wept on the bank. Then Krishna slipped free, sprang onto the serpent's raised hoods and danced upon them, stamping down every head that rose, until Kaliya vomited blood and was near death. His wives, the naga-patnis, came forward with folded hands and praised Krishna, begging for their husband's life. Krishna spared Kaliya and ordered him to return to Ramanaka Dvipa, assuring him that Garuda would not harm him once he bore Krishna's footprints.
nodes.abode: Kaliya's pool in the Yamuna; Ramanaka Dvipa
variations: The Harivamsha gives Kaliya five heads; the Bhagavata describes a hundred or more hoods, and iconography varies.
The curse of Saubhari on Garuda, explaining why Kaliya's pool was safe, is told in the Bhagavata (10.17).
Kaliya-mardana, Krishna dancing on the serpent, is a favourite subject of South Indian bronzes and temple festivals.

nodes.name: Sudama (Kuchela)
nodes.description: The poor brahmin schoolmate of Krishna at Sandipani's ashram whose visit to Dvaraka with a handful of flattened rice became the classic tale of friendship between God and devotee. The Bhagavata leaves him unnamed; the names Sudama and Kuchela come from later tradition.
nodes.story: Living in bitter poverty, the brahmin was urged by his wife to visit his old friend Krishna, now lord of Dvaraka. Having nothing to bring, he tied a few handfuls of flattened rice, begged from neighbours, in a corner of his ragged cloth. At the palace Krishna leapt from Rukmini's couch, embraced him, seated him on his own bed, washed his feet and sprinkled the water on his own head, while Rukmini fanned the guest. They talked of their days at the guru's ashram. Ashamed, the brahmin hid his gift, but Krishna pulled it out and ate a handful with delight; as he reached for a second, Rukmini gently caught his hand. The brahmin left without asking for anything, only to find on his return that his hut had become a palace and his wife was richly adorned.
symbols: flattened rice (poha, aval) in a torn cloth
variations: The Bhagavata calls him only a brahmin friend of Krishna; the name Sudama is attested in later devotional literature, and Kuchela ('one in poor clothes') is used in South India.
A different Sudama in the Bhagavata (10.41) is a garland-maker of Mathura, and Shridama is a cowherd friend of Krishna in Vraja; retellings sometimes conflate them.
Kuchela Dinam, the first Wednesday of Dhanu, is observed at Guruvayur; Porbandar in Gujarat claims to be his home town.

nodes.name: Akrura
nodes.description: A Yadava elder of the Vrishni line, son of Shvaphalka and Gandini, whom Kamsa sent to bring Krishna and Balarama from Vraja to Mathura. A great devotee, he received a vision of Vishnu in the Yamuna and later served Krishna as envoy and counsellor.
nodes.story: Ordered by Kamsa to fetch the brothers for the bow festival, Akrura set out for Vraja in rapture, longing to see the Lord. At dusk he reached Gokula, saw Krishna's footprints in the dust and rolled in them with tears. Next morning, as he drove the boys towards Mathura while the gopis wept at the parting, he stopped at the Yamuna to bathe and recite his prayers. Under the water he saw Krishna and Balarama, though he had left them in the chariot. He surfaced, saw them sitting there, and dived again: now he beheld the thousand-headed Ananta Shesha, and on his coils the four-armed Vishnu in yellow silk, attended by sages and gods. Overwhelmed, Akrura poured out a hymn of praise. When the vision faded, he returned to the chariot trembling, and Krishna asked innocently whether he had seen something wonderful.
symbols: Syamantaka jewel (held by him in some versions)
variations: Vishnu Purana 4.13 and Bhagavata 10.57: after Shatadhanva killed Satrajit, the Syamantaka came into Akrura's keeping; he left Dvaraka for a time, and famine followed until he returned.
Bhagavata 10.48–49: Krishna sent him to Hastinapura, where he consoled Kunti and warned Dhritarashtra about his treatment of the Pandavas.
The vision in the Yamuna is told at length in the Bhagavata (10.39–40) and briefly in the Vishnu Purana.

nodes.name: Uddhava
nodes.description: Krishna's cousin, friend and counsellor, a disciple of Brihaspati famed for his wisdom, who carried Krishna's message to the grieving gopis of Vraja. Before his departure from the world Krishna taught him the Uddhava Gita, the last great discourse of the Bhagavata.
nodes.story: Missing Vraja, Krishna sent Uddhava, the wisest of the Yadavas, to console Nanda, Yashoda and the gopis with a message: Krishna was never truly apart from them, being the Self of all, and they should meditate on him. Uddhava arrived proud of his knowledge. But when the gopis gathered around him, one, seeing a bumblebee, addressed it as Krishna's fickle messenger in a torrent of loving reproach, and all of them poured out such longing that Uddhava's learning seemed dry beside it. He stayed for months, listening to their songs of Krishna. Humbled, he prayed that in some future birth he might be a shrub or creeper in Vrindavan, so as to be touched by the dust of the gopis' feet, who had given up everything for Krishna. He returned to Mathura transformed by their devotion.
variations: Bhagavata 10.46–47 contains the embassy to Vraja and the Bhramara Gita (Song of the Bee); many devotional readers identify the gopi speaking to the bee as Radha.
The Uddhava Gita (Bhagavata 11.7–29) is Krishna's final teaching; afterwards he sends Uddhava to Badarikashrama.
Bhagavata Canto 3: Uddhava tells Vidura of Krishna's departure and the destruction of the Yadavas.
In the Mahabharata he is a minor Vrishni counsellor; his role grows greatly in the Bhagavata.

nodes.name: Sandipani
nodes.description: The brahmin teacher of Avanti (Ujjain), of the Kashyapa lineage, under whom Krishna and Balarama studied after Kamsa's death, mastering the Vedas, archery and the sixty-four arts in as many days. Sudama was their fellow student.
nodes.story: After Kamsa's death Krishna and Balarama, having received the sacred thread, went to live in the ashram of Sandipani at Avanti, serving him like any pupils. In sixty-four days and nights they learned the sixty-four arts, the Vedas and their limbs, and the science of arms. When they asked what fee they could offer, Sandipani and his wife, after consulting together, asked for their son, who had drowned in the sea at Prabhasa. The brothers went to the shore; the ocean told them a demon named Panchajana, dwelling in a conch shell, had taken the boy. Krishna dived in and killed the demon, but did not find the child in his body. Taking the conch, which became his Panchajanya, he went to Yama's city and blew it. Yama came out in reverence and returned the boy, whom Krishna restored to his guru.
nodes.abode: Avanti (Ujjain), where the Sandipani ashram is still shown
variations: Texts agree on sixty-four days of study but differ slightly in how the time was divided among subjects.
The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana tell the recovery of the guru's son; the Bhagavata (10.45) adds the full scene at Yama's court.

nodes.name: Jara
nodes.description: The hunter whose arrow, mistaking Krishna's foot for a deer, brought about Krishna's departure from the world after the destruction of the Yadavas. His name means 'old age', and he is not to be confused with the rakshasi Jara who joined Jarasandha's two halves.
nodes.story: After the Yadavas had destroyed one another at Prabhasa and Balarama had left his body, Krishna withdrew into the forest and lay down under a tree, absorbed in yoga, one foot resting on his knee. A hunter named Jara, prowling for game, saw the reddish sole through the leaves and took it for a deer. He loosed an arrow, which, the Bhagavata says, was tipped with the last iron fragment of the cursed pestle, swallowed by a fish and found by the hunter. Running up to claim his prize, Jara saw the four-armed Lord in yellow silk and fell at his feet in horror, begging to be killed for his sin. Krishna comforted him, telling him that all this had happened by his own will, and Jara ascended to heaven in a celestial chariot. Soon after, Krishna left the world.
variations: The Mausala Parva has Jara pierce Krishna's sole; the Bhagavata (11.30) and Vishnu Purana add that the arrowhead came from the remaining piece of the iron pestle.
A popular later tradition says Jara was Vali reborn, so that Rama's killing of Vali from hiding was repaid; this is not found in the Mahabharata or Bhagavata.
The place is identified with Bhalka Tirtha near Somnath in Gujarat.

nodes.name: Subhadra
nodes.description: Daughter of Vasudeva and sister of Krishna and Balarama, who married Arjuna and became the mother of Abhimanyu. She is worshipped with Jagannatha and Balabhadra in the triad of the Puri temple.
nodes.story: During a festival on Mount Raivataka near Dvaraka, Arjuna saw Subhadra among her attendants and fell in love. Krishna, smiling, told his friend that a svayamvara was uncertain; for a kshatriya, carrying off a bride by force was an honourable way. With Yudhishthira's consent, Arjuna waited until Subhadra went to worship at the mountain, lifted her into his chariot and drove towards Indraprastha. The Vrishnis sounded the war drums, and Balarama, furious that their guest had insulted the clan, vowed to wipe the Kurus from the earth. Krishna calmed him: Arjuna had honoured them by choosing their sister and was a match for anyone in battle; better to bring him back as a son-in-law. The marriage was celebrated, and at Indraprastha Subhadra, dressed as a simple cowherd woman, won Draupadi's affection.
variations: Texts differ on her mother: Bhagavata 9.24 makes her a daughter of Vasudeva and Devaki, while other traditions make her Rohini's daughter and so Balarama's full sister.
Bhagavata 10.86: Arjuna came to Dvaraka disguised as an ascetic, and Balarama had intended her for Duryodhana.
At Puri she is sometimes identified with Ekanamsha or Yogamaya, the goddess born to Yashoda.

edges.label: Shura (Shurasena) descends from Yadu through the Vrishni branch of the Yadavas
Shura is the father of Vasudeva
Shura is the father of Pritha (Kunti), whom he gave to his childless cousin Kuntibhoja
Vasudeva and Kunti are brother and sister, children of Shura
Vasudeva married Devaki; Kamsa drove their bridal chariot
Vasudeva is Krishna's father
Devaki bore Krishna as her eighth child in Kamsa's prison
Vasudeva is Balarama's father
Balarama was conceived as Devaki's seventh child and transferred to the womb of Vasudeva's other wife Rohini (not a node here), who bore and raised him
edges.variation: Harivamsha: the goddess Nidra made the transfer; Bhagavata: Yogamaya.

edges.label: Vasudeva is the father of Subhadra
edges.variation: Bhagavata 9.24 names Devaki as her mother; other traditions name Rohini.

edges.label: Foster father: Nanda raised Krishna in Gokula and Vrindavan
Foster mother: Krishna was exchanged for Yashoda's newborn daughter and raised by her
Nanda and Yashoda, the cowherd chief of Vraja and his wife
Close friends: Vasudeva entrusted his sons to Nanda's settlement, and Nanda met him in Mathura when paying tribute to Kamsa
Harivamsha and Bhagavata: Vasudeva is the rebirth of Kashyapa
edges.variation: Harivamsha: Kashyapa was cursed by Brahma for keeping Varuna's cows; Bhagavata 10.3 adds an earlier birth as Prajapati Sutapa.

edges.label: Harivamsha and Bhagavata: Devaki is the rebirth of Aditi, mother of the gods, so Vishnu is again born as her son
edges.variation: Bhagavata 10.3 adds an earlier birth as Prishni, wife of Sutapa.

edges.label: Cousins: Kamsa is Ugrasena's son and Devaki the daughter of Ugrasena's brother Devaka; texts often call her his sister
Kamsa imprisoned Vasudeva and Devaki and killed their newborn sons
Devaki praised the newborn Krishna as the Supreme Lord and later asked him to restore her six slain sons (Bhagavata 10.3, 10.85)
As the Vasu Drona, Nanda received from Brahma the boon of pure devotion to Hari when born on earth (Bhagavata 10.8)
As Dhara, wife of the Vasu Drona, Yashoda shared Brahma's boon of devotion to the child Hari (Bhagavata 10.8)
Bhagavata 10.8: Nanda was the Vasu Drona reborn
Yashoda's maternal love (vatsalya) is a model of devotion; she saw the universe in the child's mouth
Nanda's parental love for Krishna is celebrated as vatsalya bhakti; Krishna rescued him from Varuna and from a python
Krishna is the eighth (or ninth) avatar of Vishnu
edges.variation: Gaudiya and other Krishna-centred schools hold Krishna to be the source of all avatars (Bhagavata 1.3.28).

edges.label: Balarama is counted among Vishnu's avatars; the Mahabharata and Vishnu Purana say he came from a white hair of Vishnu
edges.variation: In some Dashavatara lists Buddha replaces Balarama.

edges.label: Balarama is the incarnation of Shesha (Ananta); at his death a white serpent left his mouth for the ocean (Mausala Parva)
Brothers, both sons of Vasudeva; Balarama is the elder, first conceived in Devaki and born of Rohini
Krishna is Subhadra's brother and helped Arjuna carry her off
Balarama is Subhadra's elder brother; he was enraged at her abduction by Arjuna
Krishna and Arjuna are Narayana and Nara reborn (Mahabharata, Vana and Udyoga Parvas)
Krishna rides Garuda against Narakasura, to Indra's heaven for the Parijata and to Banasura's city
Krishna studied the Vedas and sixty-four arts with Sandipani at Avanti
Balarama studied alongside Krishna in Sandipani's ashram
Sudama was Krishna's fellow student in Sandipani's ashram (Bhagavata 10.80)
As guru-dakshina, Krishna brought back Sandipani's drowned son from Yama's realm
Yama came out in reverence when Krishna blew the Panchajanya at his gate and returned Sandipani's son
Rukmini, princess of Vidarbha, is Krishna's first and chief queen; he carried her off on the eve of her forced marriage
Satyabhama, daughter of Satrajit, was given to Krishna after the Syamantaka jewel affair
Jambavan gave his daughter Jambavati to Krishna with the Syamantaka jewel
Kalindi, the Sun's daughter identified with the river Yamuna, became one of Krishna's eight chief queens (Bhagavata 10.58)
edges.variation: Kalindi's identification with the goddess Yami/Yamuna is traditional but not explicit in every text.

edges.label: Beloved and eternal consort: the divine love of Radha and Krishna is the heart of Vaishnava bhakti
edges.variation: Radha is absent from the Mahabharata, Harivamsha and Bhagavata; the Brahmavaivarta has Brahma marry them in the Bhandira forest, while other traditions see her love as beyond marriage (parakiya).

edges.label: Pradyumna is Krishna's eldest son
Rukmini is the mother of Pradyumna
Samba is Krishna's son
Jambavati is the mother of Samba
Aniruddha is Pradyumna's son, by Rukmi's daughter Rukmavati
Balarama married Revati, daughter of King Kakudmi (not a node), who returned from Brahma's world ages later
Aniruddha and Usha, united after Usha dreamed of him; the marriage was sealed after Krishna's war with Banasura
Arjuna carried off Subhadra from Raivataka with Krishna's approval
Subhadra is the mother of Abhimanyu
Jambavati is the daughter of the bear-king Jambavan
Rukmi and Rukmini are children of King Bhishmaka of Vidarbha (not a node)
Usha is the daughter of the thousand-armed asura Banasura
Revati's father Kakudmi descended from Vaivasvata Manu through Sharyati and Anarta
Later devotional texts say Putana was formerly Ratnamala, daughter of Bali, who wished to nurse Vamana
edges.variation: Garga Samhita and later tradition; absent from the Harivamsha, Vishnu Purana and Bhagavata.

edges.label: Kaliya is counted among the naga sons of Kadru, hence his fear of Garuda
Rukmini is revered as an incarnation of Lakshmi, Vishnu's consort
Radha is often described as a form of Lakshmi
edges.variation: Gaudiya theology inverts this: Lakshmi is an expansion of Radha, Krishna's hladini shakti.

edges.label: Brahmavaivarta Purana (Prakriti Khanda): Radha is one of the five principal forms of Mula-Prakriti, the Great Goddess
edges.variation: A Shakta-influenced view; Vaishnava schools see her as Krishna's own energy.

edges.label: Satyabhama is identified with Bhudevi, the Earth goddess
edges.variation: Regional traditions and Deepavali lore; not stated in the Bhagavata.

edges.label: Pradyumna is Kamadeva reborn after Shiva burned him
Rati, disguised as Mayavati in Shambara's house, raised Pradyumna and became his wife
In Pancharatra theology Pradyumna is the third of Vishnu's four vyuhas
In Pancharatra theology Aniruddha is the fourth of Vishnu's four vyuhas
Harivamsha and Bhagavata 10.1: Kamsa was the asura Kalanemi, slain by Vishnu in an earlier age
Bhagavata 7.1: Vishnu's gatekeepers were reborn last as Shishupala and Dantavakra; popular tradition makes Shishupala Jaya
edges.variation: Assignments of Jaya and Vijaya to each birth vary; some make Shishupala Vijaya.

edges.label: Vishnu Purana 4.14–15: the being who was Hiranyakashipu, then Ravana, was reborn as Shishupala
Vishnu Purana 4.15: Ravana was reborn as Shishupala and liberated by dying at Krishna's hand
Popular later tradition: the hunter Jara was Vali reborn, repaying Rama's arrow from hiding
edges.variation: Not found in the Mahabharata or Bhagavata.

edges.label: Krishna dragged Kamsa from his dais in the Mathura arena and killed him
Kamsa persecuted Krishna from birth, sending Putana and other demons to Vraja
The infant Krishna sucked the life out of Putana with her poisoned milk
Subdued, not slain: Krishna danced on Kaliya's hoods and banished him from the Yamuna
Spared at his wives' plea, Kaliya worshipped Krishna and went to Ramanaka bearing his footprints
Kaliya fled Garuda and hid in the Yamuna pool that Saubhari's curse forbade Garuda to enter
Krishna beheaded Shishupala with the Sudarshana discus at Yudhishthira's Rajasuya after his hundredth offence
Cousins and rivals: Shishupala lost Rukmini to Krishna and reviled him at the Rajasuya
Jarasandha besieged Mathura repeatedly to avenge Kamsa, driving the Yadavas to Dvaraka
Bhima killed Jarasandha after a fourteen-day wrestling duel at Girivraja, guided by Krishna
edges.variation: Bhagavata 10.72: Krishna splits a twig as a signal and Bhima tears Jarasandha into his two original halves.

edges.label: Krishna killed Narakasura with his discus, with Satyabhama riding beside him on Garuda, and freed 16,100 captive women
In regional tradition Satyabhama herself killed Naraka, since as Bhudevi she was the mother by whom alone he could die
edges.variation: Bhagavata 10.59 and Harivamsha: Krishna kills Naraka.

edges.label: The hunter Jara, mistaking Krishna's foot for a deer, shot him in the sole, ending his earthly life
Grieving her hundred sons, Gandhari cursed Krishna that his clan would destroy itself and he would perish alone in thirty-six years (Stri Parva)
Balarama killed Rukmi with his club after Rukmi cheated and mocked him at dice during Aniruddha's wedding
Rukmi opposed Krishna's marriage to Rukmini; Krishna defeated him and shaved his head
Krishna stopped Indra's festival and sheltered Vraja under Govardhana; later he took the Parijata tree from Indra's garden
Krishna fought Banasura to free Aniruddha and cut off most of his thousand arms, sparing him at Shiva's plea
Banasura bound Aniruddha with serpent-weapons when he was found in Usha's chambers
Duryodhana rejected Krishna's peace embassy and tried to seize him, and Krishna revealed his cosmic form in the Kuru court
After the night massacre and the attack on Uttara's unborn child, Krishna cursed Ashwatthama to wander diseased for 3,000 years (Sauptika Parva)
Krishna cursed Samba with leprosy; he was cured by worshipping Surya
edges.variation: Samba and Bhavishya Puranas only.

edges.label: Pradyumna, raised in Shambara's house, killed the demon who had stolen him as a baby
Kamsa plotted to kill Balarama with Krishna at the bow festival; Balarama slew his wrestler Mushtika
Balarama fought Jarasandha with mace and plough during the sieges of Mathura
Shishupala reviled Bhishma for proposing Krishna for the first honour at the Rajasuya
Shishupala was the suitor her brother Rukmi forced on Rukmini; Krishna carried her off on the eve of the wedding
Shachi scorned Satyabhama and refused her the Parijata flowers, prompting Krishna to take the tree (Vishnu Purana 5.30)
Satyabhama's wish for the Parijata set Krishna against Indra and the gods
Mocked by the Yadava youths who dressed Samba as a pregnant woman, Vishvamitra and his companions cursed him to bear the iron pestle that destroyed the Yadavas (Mausala Parva)
edges.variation: Bhagavata 11.1 lists a larger group of sages at Pindaraka, including Durvasa, Bhrigu, Angiras, Kashyapa, Atri and Vashistha.

edges.label: Kanva joined in the curse that Samba would bring forth an iron pestle for the destruction of the Vrishnis and Andhakas (Mausala Parva)
edges.variation: Bhagavata 11.1 lists a larger group of sages at Pindaraka, including Durvasa, Bhrigu, Angiras, Kashyapa, Atri and Vashistha.

edges.label: Narada was among the three sages whose curse made Samba deliver the iron pestle (Mausala Parva)
edges.variation: Bhagavata 11.1 lists a larger group of sages at Pindaraka, including Durvasa, Bhrigu, Angiras, Kashyapa, Atri and Vashistha.

edges.label: In the Bhagavata's version Durvasa is among the sages at Pindaraka who cursed Samba
edges.variation: Bhagavata 11.1; the Mahabharata names only Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada.

edges.label: Dvaraka tradition: Durvasa cursed Rukmini to live apart from Krishna after she drank water before offering it to him
edges.variation: Regional temple legend (Rukmini temple, Dvaraka).

edges.label: Initiated by Upamanyu, Krishna worshipped Shiva and received boons including a son, Samba, for Jambavati (Anushasana Parva)
Pleased by Krishna's hospitality, Durvasa made his body invulnerable wherever he had smeared it with payasa, except the soles of his feet (Anushasana Parva)
Without being asked, Krishna turned his poor friend's hut into a palace after eating his flattened rice
Krishna forgave the hunter who shot him and sent him to heaven in a celestial chariot
Krishna revived the stillborn Parikshit, struck by Ashwatthama's weapon in Uttara's womb (Ashvamedhika Parva)
Parvati promised Usha that she would see her future husband in a dream
Rukmi obtained the celestial bow Vijaya from Indra (Udyoga Parva)
Brahma counselled Kakudmi, after ages had passed on earth, to give Revati to Balarama
Radha is the supreme exemplar of madhurya bhakti, the loving devotion of the gopis
Sudama's selfless devotion is the model of friendship between devotee and God
Childhood friends from Sandipani's ashram; Krishna washed Sudama's feet at Dvaraka
Uddhava, Krishna's devoted cousin, received the Uddhava Gita
Krishna taught Uddhava the Uddhava Gita before leaving the world (Bhagavata 11)
Cousin, counsellor and closest friend of Krishna at Mathura and Dvaraka
Uddhava was a disciple of Brihaspati, teacher of the gods (Bhagavata 10.46)
Uddhava went to Vraja as Krishna's messenger to console Nanda, Yashoda and the gopis
Many devotional readers identify the gopi of the Bhramara Gita, who answers Uddhava's message, as Radha
edges.variation: The Bhagavata does not name her.

edges.label: Uddhava told Vidura of Krishna's departure and the end of the Yadavas (Bhagavata 3)
Akrura rolled in Krishna's footprints in Gokula and saw Vishnu on Shesha in the Yamuna
Kamsa sent his courtier Akrura to bring Krishna and Balarama to Mathura
Sent to Hastinapura by Krishna, Akrura consoled Kunti in her troubles
Akrura counselled Dhritarashtra to treat the Pandavas justly (Bhagavata 10.49)
Inseparable friends; Krishna was Arjuna's charioteer at Kurukshetra
Krishna taught Arjuna the Bhagavad Gita on the battlefield of Kurukshetra
Draupadi's sakha: Krishna protected her honour at the dice game and saved the Pandavas from Durvasa's hunger in the forest
edges.variation: The endless sari is attributed to Krishna in popular and vulgate versions; the Critical Edition's Sabha Parva does not name him in that scene.

edges.label: Krishna advised Yudhishthira on the Rajasuya and the war, and received the first honour at the Rajasuya
Satyaki, a Vrishni warrior, fought for Krishna and the Pandavas
Kunti, Krishna's paternal aunt, praised him as the Supreme Lord (Bhagavata 1.8)
Bhishma championed Krishna at the Rajasuya and praised him from his bed of arrows (Shanti Parva; Bhagavata 1.9)
Krishna chose to stay and eat at Vidura's humble house rather than Duryodhana's palace during his peace embassy
After a 28-day duel Jambavan recognised Krishna as his lord Rama and gave him the Syamantaka and his daughter
Bali welcomed Krishna and Balarama in Sutala when they came to recover Devaki's six sons (Bhagavata 10.85)
Narada visited Dvaraka and marvelled to find Krishna present in each of his queens' palaces (Bhagavata 10.69)
Draupadi instructed Satyabhama on how to keep a husband's love (Vana Parva, Draupadi-Satyabhama Samvada)
Subhadra came to Indraprastha dressed as a cowherd woman and won Draupadi's affection
Balarama taught Duryodhana mace-fighting and favoured him
Balarama taught Bhima the mace and was angered by Bhima's foul blow on Duryodhana's thigh
Balarama freed Samba from the Kauravas by threatening to drag Hastinapura into the Ganga (Bhagavata 10.68)
In-laws: after capturing Samba for abducting his daughter Lakshmana, Duryodhana gave her to him in marriage
Balarama dragged the Yamuna with his plough when she ignored his summons, until she begged forgiveness
Cured of leprosy by worshipping Surya, Samba founded a sun temple on the Chandrabhaga
edges.variation: Samba and Bhavishya Puranas.

edges.label: Relatives by marriage: Kamsa married Asti and Prapti, daughters of Jarasandha
Kamsa sent Putana to kill the infants of Vraja
Jarasandha, a devotee of Shiva (Rudra), held captive kings to sacrifice to him
Shishupala served as Jarasandha's general
Rukmi was an ally of Jarasandha and backed Shishupala's claim to Rukmini
Rukmi tried to marry his sister Rukmini to his friend Shishupala
Karna defeated Jarasandha in wrestling and received the city of Malini from him (Shanti Parva)
